newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Central banker defends Indonesian monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Central banker defends Indonesian monetary policy.

text.p: Indonesia central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said on Friday the country's monetary policy was pragmatic and ruled out the use of exchange rates to boost exports.
Djiwandono said during a two-day conference on Asian macro-economic issues that it was very tempting to classify the central bank policy as based on monetary aggregate or targeting the exchange rate.
"It is very tempting to brand our policy. But I can say our policy is pragmatic," he said.
Djiwandono declined to specify which targets the central bank was pursuing but said he did not believe in using exchange rate policy to boost the country's exports competitiveness.
"We are not a true believer in using exchange rate policy to make our exports competitive," Djiwandono said.
"It's just a supporting element, because I believe competitiveness also comes from productivity and from different kind of things."
The central bank had come under increased pressure to depreciate its currency against the dollar to boost exports and reduce rising imports of consumer goods.

Indonesia is seeking to increase exports while cutting back on imports in a bid to reduce its current account deficit, which is forecast to rise to $8.7 billion in the 1996/97 financial year (April-March) from $7 billion in 1995/96.
The rupiah had strengthened against the dollar because of an attractive interest rate differential and healthy fundamentals, the governor said.
Large-scale capital inflows had also forced the central bank to widen its dollar-rupiah trading band several times, with the last one in September to eight from five percent.

But Djiwandono declined to say whether he planned a further widening of the dollar-rupiah band. "Whether we will increase the spread or not, that is the excitement of the game. It's a mystery," he said.
Djiwandono said monetary management using traditional instruments had been less effective due to leakage in the form of capital inflows.
But he said measures had been taken to combat the problem, including regulation on banks' net open positions, commercial offshore borrowing and supervision of financial institutions.

Djiwandono said another challenge faced by Bank Indonesia was the rapid development of capital markets, bonds and stocks, whose share of the overall credit market had risen to 21 percent of total credit last August from 10.4 percent in 1990.
He said the expansion of non-bank financial systems had produced a more complex transmission mechanism between the monetary and the real (manufacturing) sector.
"The effectiveness of monetary policies has declined."
Djiwandono said more coordination of macro and micro policy would be needed to ensure effectiveness of monetary policies.
He said Indonesia's monetary management had been complicated by the fact that Indonesia is an emerging market, with funds flowing both in and out.
"If you want to depreciate and there is a huge amount of funds coming in, I think the market will laugh at us if we want to depreciate the currency," he said.
Djiwandono said the central bank would use monetary instruments to guide the market and not use them against it.
